title: A two-sided price
objectives: Quote a bid and an offer around your fair value.

screens.title: Make me a market
screens.prose: The interviewer says: "Make me a market on the sum of three dice." You think it is worth 10.5. They may buy from you or sell to you. The free guide *Probability and Markets*, written by a trading firm about its interviews, opens the same way.

state.caption: Sum of three dice: fair value 10.5

screens.question: Which pair of prices are you happy to trade at either way?

options.text: You buy at 9.5 and sell at 11.5.
You buy at 11.5 and sell at 9.5.
options.why: You put your buying price above your selling price. Whichever way they trade, you lose 1 against 10.5.

options.text: You buy and sell at 10.5.
options.why: You gave one price for both sides. Every trade at 10.5 earns nothing on average.

options.text: You buy at 3 and sell at 18.
options.why: You quoted the whole range. Nobody ever trades with you, so the answer says nothing.

hints.text: Where must your buying price sit against 10.5 for a purchase to pay?
Buy below 10.5 and sell above it.
Buy at 9.5 and sell at 11.5: each trade is 1 better than fair.

feedback.correct: Buy at 9.5, sell at 11.5: either trade earns 1 against 10.5.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. You want to buy below 10.5 and sell above it.

byKey.crossed: You would buy high and sell low. Each trade loses 1 against your own fair value.

explain.text: Buying at 9.5 a total worth 10.5 earns 1 on average. Selling at 11.5 earns 1 too. So you are content whichever side the interviewer picks.

screens.title: Two prices
screens.prose: Drag your buying price and your selling price. The caption shows what each trade earns against the fair value of 10.5.

derive.caption: They sell to you at {{b.x}}: you make {{fixed(10.5 - b.x, 2)}}. They buy from you at {{a.x}}: you make {{fixed(a.x - 10.5, 2)}}.

screens.question: When does every trade earn you something on average?

options.text: When 10.5 sits strictly between your two prices.
When both prices are above 10.5.
options.why: With both above 10.5, a sale to you at your buying price loses. Drag the buying price past 10.5 and read the caption.

options.text: When the two prices are equal.
options.why: Equal prices at 10.5 earn nothing. Equal prices anywhere else lose on one side.

options.text: Only when the two prices are far apart.
options.why: Any gap that holds 10.5 earns on both sides. A wider gap earns more a trade but trades less often.

hints.text: Drag the buying price above 10.5 and watch its line of the caption.

feedback.correct: Fair value inside the gap: both trades earn.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read both halves of the caption as you drag.

explain.text: A sale to you earns 10.5 minus your buying price. A purchase from you earns your selling price minus 10.5. Both are positive only when 10.5 sits between the two prices.

screens.title: Bid, ask and size
screens.prose: Your buying price is the **bid** and your selling price the **ask**. Traders say "9.5 at 11.5", bid first. The **width** is ask minus bid, here 2. The **size** is how many you trade at each price: "9.5 at 11.5, 3 up".
screens.question: The interviewer says "I buy 3." At what price do you sell?

widget.accept: 11.5, your ask: a buyer pays the ask.
widget.label: Price

hints.text: Is the interviewer buying from you or selling to you?
A buyer takes your ask.
They buy 3 at your ask, 11.5.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A buyer trades at the price you sell at.

byKey.bid: You used your bid. The bid is where you buy, so a seller gets it.
byKey.mid: You used your fair value. Nobody trades at 10.5; trades happen at your bid or your ask.

explain.text: The interviewer buys, so they take your ask: 3 at 11.5. You are now short 3. A buyer always pays the ask and a seller always gets the bid.

screens.title: Mark the trade
screens.prose: Interviewers ask for your P&L after every trade. Mark each trade at your fair value of 10.5, at £1 a point. The interviewer has just bought 3 from you at 11.5.
screens.question: What is your P&L at fair, in pounds?

hints.text: Each unit sold earns its price minus its value.
Three units at £1: £3.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take 10.50 from 11.50 and multiply by 3.

byKey.sign: You gave the sign of your position. You sold above fair, so the P&L is positive.
byKey.one: That is one unit. The interviewer bought 3.
byKey.cash: That is the cash you took in. Take off the value of the 3 units you owe.

explain.text: Each unit sold at 11.50 is worth 10.50, so each earns £1. Three units earn £3, and the ledger reads short 3. Say both numbers aloud after every trade.

screens.title: The larger of two dice
screens.prose: New contract: the larger of two dice. Its fair value is 161/36, about 4.47. The interviewer caps your width at 1.
screens.question: Set a bid and an ask: width at most 1, with 4.47 inside.

hints.text: Which whole numbers sit either side of 4.47?
4.47 lies between 4 and 5.
Bid 4, ask 5.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the width at most 1, with 4.47 between your prices.

byKey.crossed: Your bid is above your ask. You would buy higher than you sell.
byKey.zero: You gave zero width on an uncertain number. Any trade there is a coin flip with no edge.
byKey.too-wide: Your width is over 1. The interviewer's cap is 1.
byKey.outside: 4.47 is outside your quote. One side of it would trade at a loss.

explain.text: 4 at 5 has width 1 and holds 4.47 near its middle. A whole-number quote is quick to say and to trade. The fair value sets the centre.

screens.title: A coin game
screens.prose: The interviewer flips a coin until it shows a tail. The contract pays £1 for each head before that tail. Its fair value is £1, which the next lesson proves. Quote it with width at most 1.
screens.question: Set your quote: width at most 1, centred within 25p of £1.

hints.text: Step out the same distance either side of £1.
Width 1 means 50p each side.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Centre the quote on £1, width at most 1.

byKey.crossed: Your bid is above your ask. You would buy higher than you sell.
byKey.zero: You gave zero width. The payout is uncertain, so leave room either side.
byKey.too-wide: Your width is over 1. The cap is 1.
byKey.flips: You centred on 2, the average number of flips. The contract pays for heads only, and averages £1.
byKey.off-centre: Your quote is not centred on £1. Move both prices together.

explain.text: A fair £1 with width 1 gives £0.50 at £1.50. The payout is often 0, so the bid should stay well under £1. The centre is still the mean.

screens.title: Follow-up: a product
screens.prose: The interviewer follows up: "Now the product of two dice, width at most 2." The dice are independent, so the fair value is $3.5 \times 3.5 = 12.25$.
screens.question: Set your quote on the product: width at most 2, centred within 0.25 of 12.25.

hints.text: Width 2 means 1 either side of the centre.
The centre is 12.25.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Centre on 12.25 and keep the width at most 2.

byKey.crossed: Your bid is above your ask. You would buy higher than you sell.
byKey.zero: You gave zero width on an uncertain product.
byKey.sum: You centred on 7, the fair value of the sum. The contract pays the product.
byKey.off-centre: Your quote is not centred on 12.25.

explain.text: Independent dice let us multiply the means: $3.5 \times 3.5 = 12.25$. Width 2 then gives 11.25 at 13.25. A follow-up keeps the method and changes the contract.

screens.title: The most likely value
screens.prose: Back to the larger of two dice. A candidate sees that 6 is the most likely value. They quote 5.5 at 6.5.

state.caption: 6 is the most likely value; the mean is 4.47

screens.question: What is wrong with 5.5 at 6.5?

options.text: It is centred on the mode, so a sale to you at 5.5 loses about 1.03.
Nothing: 6 is the most likely value, so the quote should sit on it.
options.why: You centred on the most likely value. A price must match the average, and the 1s to 4s pull it down to 4.47.

options.text: It is crossed: the bid is above the ask.
options.why: 5.5 is below 6.5, so the quote is not crossed. The problem is the centre.

options.text: It is too narrow.
options.why: Width 1 is fine for this contract. The problem is the centre.

hints.text: Is the price of a contract its most likely payout or its average payout?
The mean line sits at 4.47, well left of 6.
The interviewer sells to you at 5.5 a contract worth 4.47.

feedback.correct: The centre is the mode, 6, not the mean, 4.47.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the bid with the mean.

byKey.mode: You centred on the most likely value. Over many games you are paid the average, 4.47, not 6.
byKey.crossed: 5.5 sits below 6.5, so the quote is not crossed. Look at where it is centred.

explain.text: The mean is 161/36, about 4.47, well below 6. At 5.5 at 6.5 the interviewer sells to you at 5.5, and you lose about 1.03 a unit. Centre on the mean: 4 at 5.

screens.title: A centre and a gap
screens.prose: You built every quote the same way. With fair value $\mu$ and half-width $h$: $$\text{bid} = \mu - h, \qquad \text{ask} = \mu + h, \qquad \text{width} = 2h.$$ A crossed quote, with the bid above the ask, loses on every trade.
screens.question: Four dice have fair value 14. Your half-width is 1.5. What is your ask?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the half-width to the fair value.

byKey.bid: That is your bid, 14 − 1.5. The ask sits above the fair value.
byKey.width: You added the whole width, 3. Each side sits a half-width from the centre.

explain.text: The ask is $\mu + h = 14 + 1.5 = 15.5$ and the bid 12.5. The width is 3, twice the half-width. Say it as "12.5 at 15.5".

screens.title: What the width earns
screens.prose: The interviewer sells you $q$ at your bid $\mu - h$. Later they buy $q$ at your ask $\mu + h$. Mark both trades at $\mu$.
screens.question: Write your total P&L in terms of $q$ and $h$.

hints.text: What does the purchase at $\mu - h$ earn against $\mu$?
The purchase earns $q h$; so does the sale.
$qh + qh = 2qh$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add what the purchase and the sale each earn.

byKey.one-side: That is one trade. The round trip has two.
byKey.width-each: You let each trade earn the whole width $2h$. Each earns only the half-width.

explain.text: Buying at $\mu - h$ earns $qh$ and selling at $\mu + h$ earns $qh$. Together they earn $2qh$, the width times the size. A round trip pays the market maker the width.

screens.title: Quotes in code
screens.prose: Write the quoting rule and a checker an interviewer might apply. A quote is valid when the fair value lies inside it and the width is within the limit. A known payout may have zero width.
screens.question: Complete `quote(fair, width)` and `is_valid_quote(bid, ask, fair, max_width)`.

widget.starter:
def quote(fair, width):
    """Return (bid, ask) centred on fair."""
    ...


def is_valid_quote(bid, ask, fair, max_width):
    """True when fair lies in [bid, ask] and the
    width is at most max_width."""
    ...
widget.how: Check runs 12 hidden tests. Quotes compare with math.isclose; the checker must return True or False exactly.

hints.text: The bid and ask each sit half the width from the fair value.
Python allows `bid <= fair <= ask` in one test.
Return `bid <= fair <= ask and ask - bid <= max_width`.

feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Halve the width for each side, and test both conditions.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Check that each `...` is replaced.

explain.text: `quote` puts half the width on each side, so `quote(10.5, 2)` is 9.5 at 11.5. The checker refuses a crossed quote, because `bid <= fair <= ask` fails. It also refuses the mode-centred 5.5 at 6.5.

screens.title: Quoting an option
screens.prose: You make markets in a share's call option, as in the microstructure course. Your model values the call at £4.20. The exchange lets your quote be at most 10p wide.

state.caption: Other quotes in the call; model value £4.20

screens.question: What bid do you show, in pounds?

hints.text: Your width is 10p, split across two sides.
Each side sits 5p from £4.20.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take half the width off the model value.

byKey.full: You took the whole 10p off. Each side gets half the width.
byKey.zero: You bid the model value. A trade there earns nothing.
byKey.ask: That is your ask. The bid sits below the model value.

explain.text: Half of 10p either side of £4.20 gives £4.15 at £4.25. Your quote is now the best on both sides of the book. The model value plays the part of the dice mean.

ideas: A quote is a bid and an ask around your fair value: "9.5 at 11.5" on three dice.
Centre on the mean, not the most likely value, and never let the bid pass the ask.
A round trip of size $q$ at half-width $h$ earns $2qh$; one trade earns $qh$.

formula.name: A two-sided quote
formula.note: Width $2h$. The size is how many you trade at each price.

summary.trap: Centring on the most likely value, or quoting a bid above your ask.

quiz.prose: On the sum of two dice the interviewer says: "I only want to sell. What will you pay?"
quiz.question: What is a good answer?

options.text: A bid only, such as 6, below the fair value of 7.
Refuse: a market must always have two sides.
options.why: They asked for one side. A bid alone answers it, and you can say you would show an ask too.

options.text: A bid of 8.
options.why: You bid above the fair value of 7. Each sale to you would lose 1 on average.

options.text: A bid of 7.
options.why: A bid at fair value earns nothing. Leave room below 7.

feedback.correct: A bid below 7, with the reason said aloud.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. They will only sell, so only your bid matters.

explain.text: A seller only ever meets your bid, so a one-sided price is a bid. Keep it below the fair value of 7, and say why. Offering an ask too costs nothing.

quiz.prose: A candidate quotes "12 at 10" on three dice, fair value 10.5. The interviewer sells them 1 at 12, then buys 1 at 10.
quiz.question: What is the candidate's P&L at fair, in pounds?

widget.accept: −£2: −1.5 on the purchase and −0.5 on the sale.
widget.label: P&L in pounds

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Mark each trade at 10.5.

byKey.plus: You read it as a normal quote. Here the bid is above the ask, so both trades lose.
byKey.zero: The position is flat, but buying at 12 and selling at 10 lost £2.

explain.text: Buying at 12 loses 1.5 against 10.5, and selling at 10 loses 0.5. The round trip loses £2, the crossed width. A crossed quote pays the counterparty both ways.

quiz.prose: Asked for a market on an unknown number, a candidate says "8 at 12".
quiz.question: What fair value does the quote suggest?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the middle of the two prices.

byKey.width: That is the width, 12 − 8. The fair value is the middle.

explain.text: The centre of 8 at 12 is $(8 + 12)/2 = 10$. The width is 4. An interviewer reads both from your quote.

quiz.prose: Make a market on the sum of two dice with width at most 2.
quiz.question: Which quote is best?

options.text: 6 at 8
7 at 9
options.why: You centred on 8. The fair value of two dice is 7.

options.text: 5 at 9
options.why: That has width 4. The limit is 2.

options.text: 8 at 6
options.why: Your bid is above your ask. Both trades would lose.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Centre on 7 with width 2.

explain.text: Two dice have fair value 7. Width 2 puts 1 either side: 6 at 8. The other quotes are off centre, too wide or crossed.
